headline: Hurricane Simon, 140 mph, parked off Puerto Vallarta
summary: Hurricane Simon ran up Mexico's Pacific coast on Sunday as a Category 4 storm with 140 mph winds, its eye staying just offshore. The worst was expected near Puerto Vallarta around midnight. Forecasters warn of 10 to 20 inches of rain, up to 30 in the hills, and mudslides. Jalisco cancelled school in 22 coastal towns and began evacuations.

cover_question.q: How do they know it's coming?

cover_answer: Forecasters watched it crawl at 7 mph, 65 miles out.
table_question: Would you leave your house because someone said a storm might come?

5-7.script: A huge storm called Hurricane Simon is spinning off the coast of Mexico, near a beach town called Puerto Vallarta. Its winds are 140 miles an hour, twice as fast as a car on the highway. People are moving to shelters, school is cancelled, and police with megaphones are telling everyone to stay inside. Storm scientists watch it every minute, and the grown-ups there have it.
5-7.why: A car on the highway for the wind, a megaphone for the warning.
5-7.why_long: A child this age reasons from what is in front of them, so the script gives them a car on the highway for the wind and a police megaphone for the warning, and ends on the people watching it. Expect "is it coming here?" Say where it is: Mexico's Pacific coast, and the storm scientists know where it is every hour.

8-12.script: Simon's eye is staying just offshore. Forecasters say if it never crosses onto land, it keeps its full 140 mph winds. Then the rain: 10 to 20 inches, up to 30 in the mountains, and mudslides. So Jalisco cancelled school and started moving people out. A fire drill done early: boring if nothing happens.
8-12.why: Offshore, so stronger; rain, so mud; so leave early.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect, so the script runs the chain: the eye stays offshore, so the storm keeps its strength; rain piles up in the hills, so mud comes down; so the state moves people early. The fire drill is the mechanism: it looks wasted when it works. Expect "why are tourists still going?" Some had never seen one.

13-17.script: A hotel worker remembers the Category 5 of 2002: nobody believed it would hit. "Now we're different." Simon is Category 4, 140 mph, and the housing in the hill towns may not hold. When may a government order you out of your home? Would you leave a holiday booked a year ago?
13-17.why: Two choices: the state's to evacuate, the tourist's to stay.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the resorts draw the cameras, and the people uphill in weaker housing carry the risk. The script gives them the hotel worker who remembers 2002 and the couple who had never seen a hurricane, then asks when a government may order you out. Expect "would you have left?" Answer it honestly.

5-7.q: How do they know it's coming?
5-7.a: Storm scientists track it all day. At midday it was 65 miles out, moving at 7 miles an hour, slower than a bike.

8-12.a: Forecasters say that offshore it can keep its full 140 mph strength.

8-12.q: Why are tourists still showing up?
8-12.a: Some booked long ago and had never seen one. Police told them to get inside.

13-17.q: Who's most at risk, tourists or locals?
13-17.a: Locals uphill from the resorts, the AP says, in housing that may not hold.
Jalisco is evacuating at-risk areas. Police closed the boardwalk.
